extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York; citizens, delegates, and policymakers engaged in the constitutional ratification debate
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative essays (The Federalist) articulating principles and practical standards for structuring the federal Constitution, especially the allocation of powers between the Union and the States and safeguards against usurpation. Targets readers deciding whether to ratify and advising how constitutional design should operate in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and proper / implied powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitution must include the substance of implied powers — the general authority to make use of means necessary to execute granted ends (the 'necessary and proper' doctrine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay defends the clause as indispensable: without the SUBSTANCE of this power the whole Constitution would be a dead letter. It argues that many powers cannot be executed without recourse to construction or implication and that implied powers are essential because particular means necessarily vary with the object. Avoid forms that rigidly require only EXPRESS delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of strict 'EXPRESSLY delegated' rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional rule prohibiting the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated would either disarm government of real authority or, if construed laxly, destroy the restriction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against copying the Confederation's second article (which prohibited exercise of any power not expressly delegated) because it forces a choice between absurdly narrow construction and effectively nullifying the restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticality of positive enumeration of particular means
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting a positive enumeration of all particular powers/means necessary to carry general powers into effect is infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an attempt would require a complete digest of laws for every subject and adaptations for possible future changes; particular means necessarily vary with objects, so listing them would be incomplete and quickly obsolete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of negative enumeration of exceptions ('NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER')
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to enumerate exceptions by specifying particular powers 'NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER' is chimerical and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial enumerations would likely include only powers least likely to be assumed, leaving a residuum that would be less clearly excepted; every defect in such an enumeration could operate as an unintended grant of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence would yield implication; express clause removes pretext
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Constitution had been silent about necessary means, the particular powers would result to the government by unavoidable implication; an express clause removes a pretext for questioning essential powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts the axiom that 'wherever the end is required, the means are authorized' and that explicit provision avoids plausibly arguing against essential federal authorities on critical occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for misconstruction: internal checks and popular redress
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress misconstrues its powers and exercises unauthorized authority, remedies lie first in the executive and judiciary and ultimately with the people through elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success of usurpation depends on executive and judiciary willingness to enforce legislative acts; ultimate redress is through the people electing more faithful representatives. State legislatures are likely to sound the alarm and mobilize popular opposition, making federal unconstitutional usurpation easier to check than similar state abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy of federal Constitution, laws, and treaties ('supreme law of the land')
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution, and laws and treaties made pursuant to it, must be declared the supreme law so that state constitutions cannot nullify federal authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: without supremacy, state constitutions (which vary and sometimes don't recognize Confederation powers) could annul federal authorities, produce inconsistent validity of treaties/laws across states, and invert the proper relation between head (Union) and members (States). The clause prevents fragmentation and legal contradiction among States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath of support by State officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of state legislatures and all state executive and judicial officers should be bound by oath or affirmation to support the federal Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: state officers have essential agency in giving effect to the federal Constitution (e.g., in electing the President and Senate, and administering elections), so binding them by oath secures their cooperation; a similar oath by federal officers in favor of state constitutions is unnecessary because federal officers have no role in carrying state constitutions into effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of functions: federal few/defined vs state numerous/indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers delegated to the federal government should be few and defined and exercised principally on external objects; powers remaining to the States should be numerous and indefinite, covering internal affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal operations are most important in war, peace, negotiation, and foreign commerce (and associated taxation); State powers extend to lives, liberties, properties, and internal order, improvement, and prosperity. This distribution insulates local concerns and everyday governance within State authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design as invigoration, not enlargement, of federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Constitution is characterized as invigorating the Union's ORIGINAL powers rather than creating broad new ones; only certain additions (e.g., regulation of commerce) are explicit and generally unopposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing defuses fears of overreach: many powers already vested in the Confederation are administered more effectively rather than newly conferred; tax changes shift modes of collection rather than create wholly new authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural dependence of federal government on State institutions as a safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government will be dependent on State governments and the people (e.g., in election processes), which tends to restrain federal ambition and favor deference to States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Senate elected by state legislatures; President and House depend on state structures and officers in appointment and election; fewer federal offices and less personal influence than the numerous local state offices. This dependence makes federal officers more likely to be obsequious than overbearing toward States.

rubrics_metrics.name: State advantages in numbers, personal influence, and local sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments enjoy decisive advantages in immediate dependence, local personal influence, and the sheer number of officers and contacts among citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State officers (justices of peace, militia officers, county/town officers) outnumber federal officers and are more intimately connected to the populace; in times of peace and ordinary governance the States will hold greater sway and ability to resist federal measures through local influence and legislative devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia and local governments as defense against federal standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: The militia, organized and officered under state governments, and the attachment of the people to their local governments, form a practical barrier to military usurpation by the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument includes numerical ratios (standing army likely only a small fraction of population vs militia of near half a million) and the assertion that militia officered by locally chosen men, supported by state governments, would be a formidable check on any federal attempt to use military force to subvert liberties. Thus fear of federal military usurpation is exaggerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either federal dependence on people or popular/state resistance will restrain usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: Either the federal government will be constructed so as to be dependent on the people (and thus restrained by that dependence), or it will not command popular confidence and will be defeated by state governments and the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise argument: under the first supposition dependence restrains schemes of usurpation; under the second, lack of popular confidence makes federal schemes easily defeated by State governments supported by the people. Both scenarios serve as checks on federal arrogance.
